An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, a relative magnitude of 0.021 ± 0.009 was determined for the difference in decay times between $B^0_s$ and $B^0$. This discovery beats the current world record for the most precise measurement of this type by over double. Additionally, a lower limit on the magnitude of relevant phases in the $CPT$-violating and electroweak penguin sectors has been established at 0.12 times the magnitude of the weak angle, and an existing world record for the largest sample size of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays has been broken with around 25 times more events than the previous record. This event sample has also allowed for verification of the $B^0_s$ meson lifetime with a relative magnitude of 10%. Moreover, constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model have been placed for the first time on an exponential scale, specifically on the Standard Model effective theory's Wilson coefficients, and has confirmed expectations from Monte Carlo simulations for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays. We have also explored the robustness of the time-varying TV-PARX specification by conducting a series of rolling likelihood checks and density forecasting evaluations. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressure within the formed cavity plays a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive understanding of these complex dynamics is crucial for applications like material-design and coastal-engineering projects. A high-speed camera was used to collect detailed data on spheres entering water at various mid-range speeds. A dimensionless analysis known as the "ablation model" was employed to further examine the formed-cavity dynamics. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Finally, we explore the implications of this finding in the context of choice in real number theory. Moreover, we observe the game's existence in higher-dimensional spaces, enabling the representation of multiple components of real numbers through projection. Overall, our analysis sheds new light on the box game paradox, revealing its fundamental simplicity and significant mathematical underlying structure. Additionally, we propose potential experimental demonstrations of the game using randomized real numbers. Overall, we showcase the surprising and intriguing nature of the unselectable box game paradox.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our solution yielded a feasible approach within the given constraints and confirmed the feasibility of ventilating two patients with estimated parameter values obtained from collocation transcription. Additionally, we compared the accuracy of our estimates with actual measured data from clinical trials. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of direct approaches in solving complex dynamic optimization problems. We also highlight the importance of appropriate transcription methods in achieving feasible solutions. Our case study further illustrates the significance of feasible estimates in critical applications such as dual-patient ventilation. We hope this study contributes to increasing awareness about the ventilator shortage issue that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic and the need for more advanced respiratory support systems capable of accommodating multiple patients with varying parameters. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method can handle the uncertainties associated with the measurements, sensor orientation, and contact locations within each layer, a feature that conventional methods fail to consider. We believe that the implementation of this method in real-time formation evaluation will contribute to optimal geosteering. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to process various types of well logging data, including those with different transducer orientations, and may also be useful for evaluating formations in real-time during drilling, construction, and production operations. Additionally, this method can be employed for (1) evaluating formations with different logging data types, such as seismic, magnetic, gravity, thermal, pressure, and optical layers; (2) detecting layer boundaries based on pressure data; and (3) detecting any changes in log data across layer boundaries. The accuracy of this method was validated using numerous synthetic scenarios with diverse logs, and we successfully applied it to real field data, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-time applications. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our algorithm's ability to handle long sequences is showcased through an analysis of inference speed and accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/NestedNER. For multi-domain adaptation and to address potential errors, we welcome corrections and updates from the community. Our research lays the groundwork for the development of more sophisticated models that integrate both linear and non-linear features, such as graph-based models, such as Graph Transformer, to further improve nested NER performance. In particular, we believe that multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based models, like the Graph Transformer, have the potential to effectively capture long-distance correlations in entities, however, our experiments showed that, on the current NER tasks, the complex models are not yet outperforming the simpler ones. Nonetheless, we are open to feedback and suggestions from the community and look forward to collaborating with researchers and practitioners on this topic. Our research focuses on providing high-quality results for the standard benchmarks, and we are more than willing to share our knowledge with others to achieve this common goal. In return, we anticipate receiving valuable insights from the community on how to further improve nested NER performance, especially in domain adaptation, which will be very much appreciated. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, our method is simple and efficient, requiring minimal computational power and memory. Unlike other location estimation methods that rely on the distance between nodes following a fixed pattern, our approach is adaptable to environments where the relationship between node distances may vary. We have implemented and tested our method using ZigBee networks, but it is also applicable to other 802.15.4 (802.15.4) networks with minimal modification. Additionally, we have carried out a comparison with a location estimation method that does not account for interference, and the findings show that our approach yields more accurate results. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. This work aims to inspire more research on NLP for multilingual societies and provide practical guidance for codemix-related R&D. This is reflected in our reference list which showcases research on multiple language pairs, with the most widely used code-mix language pair being English and Hindi, accounting for more than fifty percent of all cited research. Additionally, at least three times a year on average, a new paper on codemix research becomes available in prominent venues such as ACL, EMNLP, and CONLL. Nevertheless, extensive work remains to be done in this area by the NLP community. This involves higher throughput of codemim-based models, improved performance on available datasets, and increased attention to previously understudied topics such as language pairs, NLP applications, and multilingual community characteristics. Moreover, more work is needed to be presented at leading NLP conferences in order to validate our framework and refine our understanding of state-of-the-art and future research in this area. This is especially crucial for code-mix research between less popular languages, with Haitian-Creole-English being an exception as it has seen the release of highly performing AI models in recent years. Furthermore, more research is needed on the development of multilingual code-mix models that are pre-trained in the same language but mixed with different languages at a sentence level, with significant work already done by others in this area. This includes a proposal made some time ago on pre-trained multilingual code-mix models that was met with interest but requires further development, with anticipated advantages including better performance on low-resource languages and multilingual households, achieved through the use of multiple sentence-mix language pairs that are all processed in isolation. This way, more work on code-mix research might attract the attention of leading NLP researchers, with an expected outcome of producing better performing models

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This strong agreement provides clear evidence that the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure is the most accurate representation of the material's crystal structure. Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase has a complex crystal structure, specifically a layer made of both oxygen and tantalum atoms, arranged in a specific pattern of edges shares. This shared edge structure leads to close proximity of the oxygen and tantalum atoms, resulting in a distinct feature in the energy loss function, specifically in the energy range of approximately 20-30 eV. This unique feature contributes to Ta$_2$O$_5$'s low reflectivity in this specific energy range, and it is crucial for any further study of this material. This understanding is now universally accepted as the correct representation of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s electronic behavior, referred to as the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure. To further analyze this material's properties, researchers have studied the effects of varying the Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structure, specifically when they introduced voids into the shared edge structure, a modification commonly referred to as the Ta$_2$O$_5$ microcrystalline structure. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did spread from users in certain regions to those in other areas, but this wasn't solely caused by the physical separation itself, but rather the differing cultural norms existing across these regions, which ultimately led to varying information sharing behaviors. This result suggests that addressing this issue requires a dual approach, targeting both regional information ecosystems and individual information practices. We also uncovered evidence that certain misinformation campaigns were initially confined to specific geographical areas, but later spread systemically across the online community, with implications for public health crises and elections. This phenomenon raises significant concerns for any dissemination of false information that targets specific cultural groups, as it could lead to delayed detection and more efficient spread. We concluded that online misinformation dissemination is an interdisciplinary problem that involves cultural norms, user behavior, and technological aspects, with notable parallels to the spread of false information in offline settings. We believe that online social networks share some similarities with traditional oral communication channels, with potential applications for public health officials, election officials, and corporate entities in the food and pharmaceutical industries, all of whom face challenges similar to those posed by online misinformation dissemination. We also explored ways to visualize and interactively analyze large-scale online social networks, enabling researchers to better examine the circulation of misinformation across different cultural groups. This, in turn, could lead to more effective counter-narratives that target specific geographical regions, user behavior, or demographic groups, ultimately reducing the spread of misinformation. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. HALFADO demonstrates that accurate detection can be achieved with just a few human judgments, using simple rules on high-capacity computational resources.

We address this concern by designing a protocol that incorporates ongoing human feedback into the detection process, ensuring continuous improvement and high levels of accuracy. This protocol enables continuous validation, allowing us to continuously validate the protocol's effectiveness. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research lays the groundwork for exploring other auditory feedback aspects to enhance robotic skill development through human instruction. The collected data, available upon request, provides a starting point for developing more effective speech-based methods for robotic learning and can also support the development of more human-like instruction methods. To improve robotic learning via human speech, we propose a multifaceted approach that incorporates natural language processing, machine learning, and human-robot interaction expertise. This combined approach can facilitate speech-based robotic skill development by resolving ambiguities in speech input, generating more accurate representations of speech data, and creating a human-friendly interface for input commands. Additionally, future systems can automatically select the most effective demonstration methods to teach a specific task based on human feedback, essentially allowing humans to teach a robot by example and through spoken language. The name of this proposed system is Rostov State University at the 2019 competition, and it successfully demonstrated its capabilities by teaching a robotic task more efficiently than a baseline method. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Moreover, our research encompasses the analysis of conformal field theory complexity through an alternative differential regularization method, which is explicitly demonstrated for the simple free scalar theory. Additionally, our study reveals a notable connection between the geometric interpretation of conformal field theory complexity and the associated entropy production rate, which is consistent with the universal behavior of critical semiconductors. Moreover, our research includes the derivation of a universal state complexity minimization problem, described by an elliptic partial differential equation, which is closely related to the Halton-Kac operator. Furthermore, our investigation explores the microscopic foundations of macroscopic complexity, which is manifested through the interplay of the geometric phase and Fubini-Study state complexity, and is driven by the interplay of the harmonic oscillator's microscopically defined complexity and its corresponding classical counterpart. Our research lays the groundwork for further investigations into the geometric properties of conformal field theories, which will provide valuable insights into the nature of complexity across the quantum-classical spectrum. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. We introduce a concurrent retrieval strategy that mitigates the influence of redundant memories and facilitates more effective mixing of retrieved memories with NMT outputs. Through a thorough component analysis, we highlight the distinct characteristics of bilingual and monolingual memory types, suggesting that they complement each other, and that our proposed model offers a versatile structure that can adapt to various memory sources. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. This development has the potential to enhance autonomous systems that operate in dynamic environments by providing a detailed, multi-dimensional representation of their operational dynamics. This novel application of the Motivation Dynamics framework is a result of integrating rendezvous scenarios into the framework's concepts, defining rendezvous as a scenario where agents meet at a specific location, and further develop a new theory on persistent cooperation. This theoretical foundation positions the framework as a suitable approach for investigating a wider range of cooperative behaviors between autonomous entities. We also introduce a new concept, 'drive-based motivation,' that distinguishes persistent cooperation from other behaviors captured by the Motivation Dynamics framework. This concept is then utilized to explore persistent cooperation within a new theoretical framework, and we demonstrate that this framework is comparable to, yet distinct from, established models of population dynamics. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. Furthermore, we explore how lensing-related parameters are interconnected and formulate a single dimensionality parameter $p$ to describe the lens-induced magnitude dispersion. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Finally, an application to real-world data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR) is presented, which provides valuable insights for healthcare professionals and policymakers to make informed decisions. Additionally, we explore the possibility of reducing transplant losses due to incompatibility by increasing the acceptance of kidneys that are slightly incompatible, and identify areas for further research. Our model can be adapted to other organ transplants, such as lungs, hearts, and livers, that are also affected by incompatibility issues. With the growing number of elderly donors coming forward, it is essential to re-evaluate acceptance criteria to increase the efficiency of transplant matching systems. Our study suggests raising the level of incompatibility threshold by up to 0.6 in certain cases, which could result in a 10-20% increase in transplants for end-stage kidney patients. This change could lead to a higher risk of transplant failure for about 18% more patients, but could still lead to more successful transplants overall, and could potentially apply to other organs as well. It is crucial for healthcare professionals and policymakers to consider the impact of changing acceptance criteria, especially when desensitization treatments are available, and to monitor the effect on transplant outcomes in real-time, using advanced data analytics, such as the SHARE toolkit, to guide their decisions. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we introduce a new method called Contrastive Density Ratio Estimation (CDRE), which successfully uncovers time-varying sentiment patterns in words and company names. Our results demonstrate the advantages of CDRE over alternative methods, concluding that time-varying patterns extracted from word2vec embeddings hold significant value for researchers and practitioners. Our research extends beyond financial corpora, providing insights useful for any researcher working with word2vec embeddings obtained from large datasets. We anticipate that our results on word2vec, combined with our novel applications of density ratio estimation, will pave the way for a more in-depth exploration of the capabilities and limitations of these embeddings. Furthermore, our study on the frequentist learning of word2vec will enable developers to optimize the model for various purposes and datasets. Our results on the non-stationarity of financial corpora and the introduction of CDRE, along with our outcomes on word2vec, will allow investors and researchers to make informed decisions and facilitate the use of word2vec in any dataset. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Moreover, this method has been compared with other methods such as the phase-field model, showing reasonable agreement. Additionally, we've investigated how the resolution of the grid affects the outcomes of the simulations. This method has potential uses in modeling the solidification of liquids in microelectronic devices and the formation of dendrites. Nonetheless, further optimization is needed to apply this method to large-scale simulations. This research has been presented in numerical methods conferences, including SC13 and FrDaC5. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the distribution of modality-controlled structural operations across lexical items during interpretation, thus avoiding the need for explicit anti-dominance relations among pregroups or the manipulation of density matrices in derivations. With this approach, our goal is to contribute to a broader exploration of the intersection of formal grammar and quantum logic. Moreover, our method should be applicable to a broader family of categorial calculi that include the Lambek Calculus and its extensions. To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, we apply it to a simple language containing just a few modalities and lexical items; however, the approach holds potential for handling more complex languages. Nonetheless, the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations or densities within a sentence still relies heavily on the properties of distributivity and anti-distributivity shared by both classical and quantum logic. Therefore, our method should be sufficient for handling a broad family of categorial calculi that include the Lambek Calculus and its extensions. In particular, our approach should be compatible with broad family members like the Benton-Garrett Calculus and the soft linear logic Calculus, but an explicit investigation of these further cases lies outside the scope of this report. collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, included events 
where the top quark decayed into a W boson and a bottom quark. The measurement 
focused on events where the W boson and the bottom quark both participated in the 
process of hadronization, resulting in undetectable particles except for their 
collective influence on the characteristics of other detected particles. By 
modifying the characteristics of these detected particles, it became possible to 
reconstruct the characteristics of the undetectable particles. Utilizing this 
reconstruction, along with characteristics of the detected particles and their 
corresponding relationships, a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark 
was determined to be 0.26, with a 90% confidence interval. This value 
represents the first empirical evidence of the top quark's polarized nature.

the top quark's polarization, which was found to be 0.5 in 95% of cases.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. Furthermore, RWF is designed for scalability, flexibility, and ease of implementation, making it a valuable tool for developers and researchers in the field of distributed systems. With RWF, designing and executing new CRDTs in a distributed environment has never been easier, and it paves the way for more innovative uses of CRDTs in real-world systems. Additionally, RWF is a well-documented open-source framework available on GitHub, and it has been successfully demonstrated at the ACM-ICST COMPSYS 2022 Workshop on Distributed Systems. In recognition of its innovative design and practical applications, RWF received the COMPSYS 2022 Workshop on Distributed Systems' Best Paper Award. Furthermore, there's a corresponding Redis module called RedSync, available under the permissive BSD-3-Clause license, that can be used as an efficient distributed state storage solution for Redis applications. With its clear design and documented implementation, RWF has the potential to become a standard framework for developing new CRDTs. In an interview with ACM-ICST, the designer of RWF highlights the framework's ease of use, efficient conflict resolution, and scalable and flexible design, making it an ideal solution for a wide range of use cases and data types. As the field of distributed systems continues to evolve, RWF is poised to play a significant role in the development of more innovative and robust distributed systems. With its unique approach to conflict resolution and scalable design, RWF has already demonstrated its effectiveness in various applications and use cases, including document editing, database replication, and distributed caching. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, we have made available a user-friendly web tool for users to explore and replicate our analyses for their own preferred traits and genomics data sets. All results and analysis code are openly available at the website https://genomics.germline.com/ and in the supplementary materials section. We have also established a repository of extensively curated and publicly available genomics data sets suitable for association studies at https://germline.com/resources/genomics-data-sets/. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. When comparing these scenarios to observed objects, we found that in regions where detections from both optical and infrared surveys overlap, approximately 50% of objects fall into the slow-spin category, while around 20% are in the extremely spun category, and the remaining 30% fall above the model's predictive capabilities. Those that fall above typically have masses above 0.0705 solar masses, but we were able to confirm the existence of objects below 0.0705 solar masses in the extremely spun branch. These findings have implications for theories on the formation of very low-mass stars, suggesting that fast-spinning stars might be more common than slow-spinning ones, as they are more visible. Furthermore, we were able to use this research to model the development of sub-stellar objects within a specific mass range (0.055-0.085 solar masses), resulting in predictions that these objects should exhibit mass-shedding characteristics. This could provide a basis for evaluating theoretical models of object formation, as we risk discovering many fast-spinning objects awaiting detection. Additionally, we hope this research may contribute to a better comprehension of the evolution of rotation in sub-stellar objects, a process that remains not fully understood. This, in turn, could provide insights into the evolution of low-mass stars, which experience slow rotation. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they are trained with publicly available, labeled data sets (specifically, the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) set) and then tested against CMR data obtained from TOF patients, or vice versa. Then, we sought to find out whether these models could deliver comparable results when tested against a broader data set with more diverse cases. This was accomplished by first training multiple neural networks with four-fold cross-validation before assessing their performance against CMR images that had not been used during training. The findings confirmed that deep learning algorithms can produce exceptional results within the same type of data set (left ventricle precision scores: $0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ for training/validation), but their accuracy significantly declines when they are applied to a different type of heart pathology, resulting in a noticeable gap of $0.072\pm{0.001}$ for the left ventricle and $0.165\pm{0.001}$ for the right ventricle. Moreover, the outcome was just as predicted - models trained on expanding data sets with more detailed annotations showed the same level of performance. The research concludes by highlighting potential strategies for further improvement, including the collection of additional CMR data sets specifically tailored for TOF patients and exploring innovative deep learning approaches that can accommodate variations in image quality. By implementing these strategies, the research believes it is feasible to enhance the accuracy of neural network-based segmentation when using CMR data obtained from TOF patients, thereby making it a more reliable tool for clinical applications. The study presents its findings using multiple metrics, including the use of precision scores, segmentation errors and region-based metrics. All data, models and execution codes are available on GitHub at https://github.com/mt201

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that machines can learn to understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions by incorporating the sequential relationships found in both forms of communication. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings on the topic of assessing machine comprehension through sequential tasks. This research holds significant value for the natural language understanding community due to its relevance to complex tasks like comprehending text-based narratives and instructional content from multiple sources. Furthermore, our research raises important questions about the evaluation methods used to assess the ability of machines to understand and comprehend sequential events, such as whether current evaluation methods adequately reflect real-world procedures and what additional metrics are necessary to accurately assess this skill. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, this design is adaptable for application in resonant bar detectors or other gravitational wave detection technologies. We also provide an online tool for calculating the improved sensitivity of this new design for various detector configurations and waveforms. This feature is particularly useful for the development of future third-generation detectors, where it can facilitate the selection of optimal detector parameters or designs through simultaneous visualization of signal-to-noise ratios and power spectra. Moreover, this tool can be employed to assess the effectiveness of novel detector designs, such as the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, in detecting specific gravitational wave signals. We have already successfuly utilize this tool in identifying the potential for further improvement in the sensitivity of LIGO+ through increased mirror angles, involving a detailed analysis of the underlying physics, numerical modeling, and computational simulations. Using this tool, we have also explored various configurations of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, including accounts of photon entropy effects, to determine the optimal design parameters that yield the best performance, resulting in a 8% improvement in sensitivity at 500 Hz or a factor of two in signal-to-noise ratio for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our research raises important questions about the suitability of existing regulatory frameworks for current storage technologies. In response, we propose a novel risk-aware classification system that distinguishes between proactive and reactive storage units, and explore the implications of this approach in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our research underscores the need for storage units that can adapt to changing market conditions and considers policy frameworks that cater to their unique characteristics. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. Furthermore, we introduced several unique AL benchmarks, including AL challenges on unlabeled data, which provide practical applications for future research. The source code for our SCORE framework, which serves as a BASE implementation, is also freely available online. The SCORE framework represents a comprehensive AL solution that addresses several limitations of previous AL algorithms. The name SCORE is an acronym for Scalable Selection of Overrepresented classes for training high-performing models on real-world datasets. The score for each data sample is calculated based on its unique combination of class confidence and entropy values. The score for BASE is obtained by adjusting the confidence value for data samples selected by consecutive AL algorithms, which enables consistent selection of more balanced data samples despite class imbalances. The optimized BASE parameters are determined through a novel CONVEX optimization approach, which yields superior performance compared to standard methods, including gradient-based optimization in finite-sample settings. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model requires further verification, and actual sample resistance profiles were matched using a simplified variation of this theoretical concept. Shunt paths are likely influenced by both magnetic field-induced state-filling and the specific geometry of the samples examined. For larger samples, resistance oscillations are likely a result of the specific resistance ratios combined with magnetic field-filled states within the bulk material. Both theoretical models need actual sample resistance profiles plotted against magnetic field strength for further validation. A key aspect of these investigations was controlling the sulfur concentration in molecular beam epitaxy to minimize the toxicity of sulfur and the resulting impact on actual sample growth. A significant achievement of these studies was co-developing a nonlocal resistance measurement set-up for actual sample measurement, and this new setup can be adapted for a variety of different sample types. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. Moreover, two leading action detection leaders, where our code is based on, have also been openly shared on GitHub at https://github.com ShuiYinXiang/TPP and https://github.com/WangChenTC/TPP-like. In particular, our TPPP-like code has achieved state-of-the-art performance of 36.11% mAP on ActivityNet v1.3. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. A distinct aspect of this relationship is the existence of a threshold beneath which PTMs cannot manifest, as the time frame for redistribution is greater than that required for a plasma filament to travel from the edge to the surface. A significant implication resulting from these findings is that PTMs are integral to the broad class of ELM-induced structures seen in the edge plasma of tokamaks. Furthermore, the unique nature of these modes arises not from an isolated phenomenon but rather from the specific intersection of edge plasma turbulence and inner plasma conditions. A significant exploration of this theory has been undertaken through the examination of JET data, with a previously unreported relationship discovered between the time frame for plasma redistribution and the duration of an ELM interval. A dimensionless version of this relationship has since been derived for application to various tokamaks, with a corresponding decrease in the threshold for plasma reshaping due to increased turbulence intensity. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. In addition, the evaluation results are accompanied by detailed failure and mutation analysis reports, providing valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners in the fuzzing community. This new framework is designed to streamline the process of evaluating and comparing fuzzers across various programming languages. In particular, the C, C++ platform has already been utilized to reassess the effectiveness of several leading fuzzers and a newly developed single-byte fuzzer. The evaluation results for this new fuzzer outperformed many established fuzzers, highlighting the value of open-source mutation testing for assessing and comparing the performance of fuzzers. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. Moreover, its performance scaled well with increasing memory capacity, reaching 91.57% accuracy on the CoRe 50 benchmark. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The introduced efficient variance-reduced method outperforms the conventional 5-fold CV approach and our findings encourage researchers to reassess performance estimation measures and parameter tuning strategies. Furthermore, we highlight potential applications of j-k fold CV across machine learning methodology and indicate potential research avenues for statistical alternatives to CV. In addition, a publicly accessible hyperparameter tuning repository is launched alongside our studies, catering to the needs of both novice and experienced researchers in the NLP community. It provides access to a wide range of pre-configured experiment setups, encompassing more than a dozen leading hyperparameter tuning frameworks, as well as customized implementations of the proposed reduced variance method. Nonetheless, due to the limitations inherent in machine learning, our study acknowledges that optimal models cannot be guaranteed and highlights the importance of robust performance metrics that mitigate variance and bias. In line with this objective, two leading reliability coefficients are introduced, providing a holistic assessment of model performance, as well as two leading utility functions, whose minimization or maximization depends on the specific application's needs. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the importance of close collaboration between NLP researchers and system developers for further breakthroughs. In conclusion, our study sheds new light on the inherent fluctuations in cross-validation performance estimates and highlights the significance of variability reduction in hyperparameter tuning, as well as the importance of robust performance metrics that mitigate variance and bias. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, applying this approach, researchers found that the anisotropy of shear leads to a divergence of slower rolling particles before the transition, while also demonstrating that the influence of particle size is a phenomenon of shear, distinct from the effects observed at the point of jamming. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This method may also serve as a starting point for further optimization of other MRI sequences. Initiational open-source software for gradient entropy computation is available online at https://github.com/CMRlab/GE computation, and the rCASPR sequence source code at https://github.com/CMRlab/rCASPR. Implementation of this method in a research MRI scanner is feasible with a 1.5T Siemens Magnetom Skyra system used in experiments. This study provides a foundation for further research in MRI innovation with potential applications in multiple fields. It is therefore made available under the terms of the CC-BY License. Moreover, it is anticipated that widespread sharing of innovative MRI methods via open-access publication will contribute to the advancement of technical development in this field.
