A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Finally, a guide on how to access and utilize this dataset, along with instructions for replicating the statistical findings, is presented for the benefit of academic researchers. 

The container shipping data sets comprise six primary routes: Far East to US East and West Coasts, Europe to US East and West Coasts, Far East to UK, Europe to US East and West Coasts, South America to US East and West Coasts, and Australia/New Zealand to US West Coast. Each monthly data point includes the average freight rate in US dollars per 40-foot equivalent units (TEUs), total shipping quantity in TEUs, new building prices in US dollars per TEU, used scrap prices in US dollars per TEU, and average used secondhand prices in US dollars per TEU. 

To combine the data sets from various sources, the following steps are followed. First, the used scrap price is considered the most reliable data point as it is least susceptible to manipulation and pricing fluctuations. Second, used secondhand prices are derived from new building prices and are subject to change based on market conditions. Third, shipping quantity is constructed by reversing the process used for new building prices. Fourth, freight rate data is validated through a regression analysis that incorporates the data sets from various sources. 

The container crisis of 1974-1975 served as the primary event analyzed using the data sets. Descriptive statistics reveal distinct patterns in market behavior during this period. Furthermore, the research demonstrates how the structural changes in market variables contributed to a better understanding of this crisis.

These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. Ultimately, this study sheds new light on the capabilities and limitations of linear sketches in the face of adaptive inputs. A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that induces a thermal gradient. This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy ratio in the vortex liquid, which in terms of units $\frac{\hbar}{k_B}$, is much greater than what is observed in common liquids. Moreover, there's a distinction to be made between the entropy held within the vortex core and the entropy bound to a moving magnetic flux line. A crucial aspect to consider here is that the entropy within the vortex core undergoes a continuous exchange with the surrounding normal quasi-particles due to a normal steady flow, which causes a decrease in the entropy bound within the core as the vortex moves at a slower speed. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/benjamin501/Real-time-Aggregation. The investigation into MEF properties, its implementation through reinforcement learning, and resulting performances of the proposed PPC provide valuable insights for the management of adaptive load aggregates. The study assumes a centralized planning framework and focuses exclusively on the MEF of individual aggregators, without addressing issues of trust and security in critical infrastructure. The results, however, suggest promising applications for our approach in addressing similar challenges elsewhere in complex multi-agent systems. The study also implies that the incorporation of learning-driven methods can mitigate difficulties associated with traditional approaches, such as the necessity for precise initial conditions, with the MEF framework allowing for tolerance to certain deviations. The study extends beyond conventional power systems, with potential applications arising in energy systems that involve multiple interconnected layers, such as heat and power co-generation systems, hydraulic systems, and other complex, interconnected networks, especially those with slowly dynamic components that can be reconfigured. The study explores the possibility of adapting and reconfiguring existing infrastructure to accommodate new levels of controllability, with the MEF framework providing a means for capturing these aggregate flexibility capabilities in real-time. The study investigates the possibility of combining weather forecasts with real-time feedback, with the MEF framework allowing for the incorporation of such adaptations in real-time. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This research introduces a new conservation principle based on the specific details of common envelopes, which involves the conservation of initial and final total potentials, as well as an new invariant that predicts the outcome of these processes. This new invariant shows that in binary star systems, the common envelope phase will always result in a merger, which demonstrates the complexity of these systems through the derivation of a simple and intuitive equation. This equation displays a fascinating symmetry, which arises due to the unique characteristics of these binary star systems. This research also reveals the critical role that conservation of angular momentum plays in predicting the outcome of common envelopes, especially in systems that are tidally synchronized, or in systems that involve a white dwarf, as these processes result in the conservation of angular momentum, which in turn leads to the ejection of the common envelope in these specific cases. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. We developed a theoretical model that accurately predicts the anisotropy and the influence of the speed at which the cylinder is moved and its dimensions. This model may be applicable to a wide range of situations in which loose material rubs against solids moving through it. We also found that the drag experienced by the cylinder moving through a bed of grains is a key factor in the motion of objects moving through sand, particularly in situations where loose material accumulates on the surfaces of moving objects, a phenomenon known as sandblast. This is particularly common in the motion of swimming animals that move quickly through water filled with sediment. This phenomenon is important because it cannot be understood or predicted using existing theories. We propose a new method for studying this phenomenon experimentally and several possible ways this could be accomplished. This involves building a large tank that can withstand high speeds of flow and accurately measures the drag experienced by the cylinder moving through it at high speeds. This could also involve collaborating with experts in biology, ecology, and medicine to design the experiment in a way that accurately represents the conditions experienced by swimming animals moving quickly through water filled with sediment. This could include using a heart that pumps water through the tank at high speeds, a body that the swimmer is moving through water filled with sediment, and various types of swimmers to study how different types of friction experienced by the swimmers affect the drag experienced by the cylinder moving through the water filled with sediment. This could also involve looking at the economy and living standards of the region where the experiment is being conducted to design the experiment in a way that accurately represents the conditions experienced by swimming animals moving quickly through water filled with sediment in that region.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. Furthermore, BoAnon's code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hpcresearch/boanon. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric called efficient improvement ratio (EIR), which provides a clear understanding of BoAnon's efficiency in finding optimal configurations within a given time frame. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. The model's performance is remarkable, with only a small percentage of generated scenes being deemed unusable. Overall, SceneGen yields a substantial increase in the accuracy of simulated scenes and reduces the need for expensive real-world data collection. As a result, SceneGen is an important advancement in the field of self-driving vehicles and has significant implications for industries beyond transportation. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, the proposal is evaluated in conjunction with an explicit time-stepping method for the one-dimensional Allen-Cahn equation. Key aspects of the modified iteration method are also discussed in an abstract framework. Additionally, this study investigates the effects of different preconditioning techniques on the proposed iteration method. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the method's performance. Although the proposed iteration method retains the convergence properties of the flexible GMRES method, further work is needed to establish its theoretical convergence properties. The study is concluded with an examination of potential directions for future research. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/yangyangdai/far3det. Our research lays the groundwork for further investigation into the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors in far-field three-dimensional detection. We hope this study will pave the way for more expert researchers to explore this challenging problem. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We anticipate our benchmark to contribute significantly to the development of advanced scene flow algorithms. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Additionally, our findings highlight the significant impact of the population's spatial distribution on its controllability. Specifically, we show that when the population's mean mobility rate exceeds a critical threshold, it becomes controllable via localized action; otherwise, it remains uncontrollable via localized action. Our approach to achieving null controllability builds upon a strategy introduced by F. Ballerini and E. Zuazua in their 2018 study. Moreover, our results complement the findings presented by G. N. Gatica, R. OlerMarquez, and J. G. Pérez in their 2019 paper. Notably, our results reveal that in scenarios where the population's mean mobility rate is marginally sufficient to achieve controllability, the associated control norm exhibits a sublinear relationship with the population's initial magnitude; whereas, for populations with mobility rates substantially greater than the required minimum, the associated control norm exhibits a linear relationship with the population's initial magnitude. Our research further extends the results presented by G. N. Gatica, R. OlerMarquez, and J. G. Pérez in their 2019 paper by accounting for the population's spatial distribution. Ultimately, our work emphasizes the importance of balancing the complexity of the proposed evaluation tasks to ensure they accurately reflect the underlying representation of encoding user input for the next utterance. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. We validate our theoretical model by comparison with experimental measurements of thermal capacity in doped graphene sheets obtained from hydrogen-saturated samples. Adjusting for hydrogen bonding does not require alignment and we find the velocity of charge carriers to be approximately 10% higher than predicted by a basic model of graphene. This outcome indicates that a simple free-electron model is sufficient to describe the low-energy dynamics of Dirac electrons in doped graphene sheets. Nonetheless, at higher temperatures or low doping levels, the thermal capacity displays an increase more rapid than linear due to the formation of a thermal distribution of energies around the Fermi level. This phenomenon is a general consequence of interactions within a class of normal Fermi liquids. We also examine the compressibility of doped graphene and find it to be a non-interactive free-electron model's prediction, with a finite charge susceptibility at finite temperatures resulting from a combination of zero-point fluctuations and thermal effects. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that hollow atoms reside on both sides of doped graphene sheets and contribute significantly to its electronic properties. We refer to these atoms as a graphenium shell and speculate that they may also influence the electronic properties of doped h-BN layers. Furthermore, we explore the electronic property modifications that arise when a single layer of a transition metal is placed on top of doped graphene or h-BN. These modifications include a significant reduction in the carrier velocity of charge carriers, potentially due to a failure in a direct comparison of our theoretical model with an experimental measurement of thermal capacity in Co-overlayer graphene. A more detailed analysis of this phenomenon is a subject for future research. We predict that this failure might also lead to an increase in the velocity of charge carriers in a Co-overlayer doped graphene if the direct comparison is unsuccessful. Conversely, when a full band is considered, the velocity of charge carriers in Co-overlayer doped graphene is actually lower than in graphene, potentially due to a failure in a direct comparison of our theoretical model with an experimental measurement of thermal capacity in Co-overlayer graphene.

These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Evaluation results reveal that MaskedSpeech excels in both metrics, achieving a mean score improvement of 0.17 in naturalness and 0.13 in expressiveness. Moreover, MaskedSpeech demonstrates flexibility in data configuration, showcasing potential as a context-aware synthesis framework. The source code of MaskedSpeech is available online at https://github.com/xiaofengV/MaskedSpeech. Analysis of the embedding space using visual tools reveals that MaskedSpeech develops a more context-aware semantic map than baseline systems. Furthermore, MaskedSpeech's ability to process long contexts through chaining correlations stems from its coherent semantic map. The examination of masking strategies' effects on semantic maps and synthesis quality is a subject for future study. the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. High-level code for our ensemble method is freely available at
https://github.com/cygnus1/SCA-ensemble, along with pre-trained models at

the challenging case datasets categorized by contextualized methods at
https://github.com/cygnus1/SCA-ensemble-data. The term "semantic change" has
different meanings depending on the context in which it is used. For

word meaning that stays constant across varying contexts. To avoid further
confusion and clarify our scope, we define our task as the practical
problem of identifying the degree of semantic change in word meanings that
stay consistent across contexts. With that said, we acknowledge that the
challenge of semantic change detection encompasses all the aforementioned
aspects. The degree of semantic change in words can be understood as the

the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to other

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The TKS dataset can be accessed through the Keck Observatory Archive and the Exoplanet Archive of the California Planet Search, respectively. Additionally, the survey has the potential to contribute to the development of theoretical models predicting the characteristics of planets in various contexts. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. We also identified clusters of users who collaborated, with some communities emerging only if initial commenters stirred reaction from others. Communities within politics exhibited distinct behavioral patterns, with some communities consisting of users who repeatedly clashed, while others were marked by harmony and agreement. To further analyze these online discussions, we developed a dataset comprising co-interaction networks, available for researchers to explore. We hope this dataset enables research exploring topics such as community behavior, online influence, and the dissemination of information on social media platforms. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. Furthermore,
we introduce an indirect method for calculating decay widths via off-shell form
factor calculations, utilizing a two-body initial state rather than the usual off-shell
process, which is also demonstrated in this study. Although the indirect method
yields a comparable result to the known full-spectral width, our current capacity is
limited by a signal-to-background ratio issue. In order to enhance this, we suggest
increasing the reconstruction cutoff threshold or exploring alternative methods
for decay width calculations. In the case of $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$, the proposed
direct method proves to be more efficient in signal extraction. Additionally, we
investigate the decay width of the $B$ meson, resulting in an upper limit of
$10.3$ pb for the branching fraction, which falls short of the world experimental
value. Moreover, we derive the form factor for $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$ at zero-momentum transfer.

However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Nonetheless, the neutralization of the sign problem comes at the expense of introducing nonphysical trial wave functions, whose effect can be quantified and mitigated further. Our framework is particularly suited for simulations dealing with discrete bosons, fermions, and Lie transport, as demonstrated by our test simulations of the 2D Hubbard model and dynamical mean-field theory, which showcase the robustness of this approach. The source code of our project is openly available at https://github.com/sign-problem-solvers/spsm. Additionally, the framework has been incorporated into the interface of the ALF (Algebraic Free Fermion) algorithm, which is also made publicly available at https://github.com/alf-algorithm/ALF. This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  We have made progressive releases of ATOMIC, referred to as ATOMIC-V1 to V3, in an effort to address issues of imbalance within the dataset.  Our response to these concerns involved expanding the dataset in areas where it was limited through an open call for contributions.  A crucial aspect of the expanded dataset is the presence of diverse conditional relationships that were absent from the original collection.  These additional relationships shift the overall balance of the dataset, resulting in a more comprehensive representation of the range of conditional relationships that people hold as common sense.  We intend to continue developing ATOMIC through further research aimed at defining a standardized framework for describing these relationships and developing more precise methods for assessing the accuracy of these descriptions within the context of the dataset.  We have already initiated exploratory work in this area and are willing to share our progress with others in the field.  Machine learning models trained on ATOMIC or its expanded versions perform significantly better than baseline models in a variety of tasks that rely on commonsense reasoning, including filling in missing components of if-then relationships, predicting one aspect of a relationship when the other is known, predicting one part of a double causal link, and evaluating the accuracy of descriptions of these relationships.  We have investigated multiple approaches to training these models, including the effectiveness of incorporating the dataset's descriptive language, the balance of its examples, and its impact on model performance over time.  Our research into these topics has involved a range of machine learning models, over 800,000 training examples from ATOMIC, over 30,000 evaluation examples from the test set, and over 1,000 examples from each of the nine categories that make up the dataset. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. The findings provide actionable insights for the development of multiple application domains, such as chemistry and materials science, cryptography, machine learning, and optimization. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Additionally, we introduce the concept of unclonable encryption with an unlearnable function and present two novel constructions meeting this standard, which could have implications for new copy-protection schemes. Our findings are the result of integrating ideas from both Broadbent and Lord's work and our own research on unclonable functions, building upon both foundations. Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of the
star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can lead
to observable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It discusses the need for further interdisciplinary
research, fueled by the growing interest in hosted planets in compact binaries and
the impending launch of new telescopes and missions that will revolutionize our
understanding of stellar and planetary magnetospheres and winds. This review also
highlights the importance of computational modeling in both stellar and planetary
physics, as well as the potential for cross-fertilization of ideas and methods. It
concludes with the promise of studying both stars and planets as part of a wider
universe, using the tools provided by the advancing launch of new telescopes and
missions. This review is the outcome of the workshop 'Winds and Magnetospheres of
Stars and Planets: Similarities and Differences' held in Rome on March 15-17, 2022,

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This understanding may pave the way for discovering the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in other material combinations. Additionally, the findings of this study can be applied to improve the magnetic anisotropic resistance in Bi/Co multilayers, a phenomenon previously attributed to an intrinsic mechanism. This knowledge may be utilized to design novel spin-orbit coupled systems with magnetic anisotropic properties. Furthermore, the discovery of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Bi/Co multilayers may provide a means to incorporate magnetic anisotropic properties into non-magnetic materials through proximity effect. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Moreover, designers can proactively mitigate beam breakup by incorporating specific filling patterns that incorporate beam-RF coupling factors and mode acceptance values of the RF cavities. This approach contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of beam breakup instability across various filling patterns and multiple pass energies, fostering more effective use of current and future energy recovery linac capabilities. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Furthermore, it provides the ability to classify targets employing the results of reduced dimensionality, and the package is compatible with Bioconductor for handling genomic data. The LFDA R package is available on CRAN and Bioconductor, catering to users and developers alike. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code for our work is publicly available at https://git.io/JgkGf.

In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. All helicity configurations for this process have now been investigated. In contrast to previous findings, certain heavy-quark results show that even under a NMRK quark and antiquark splitting limits, the two-gluon CEV cannot be fully described by product-like relationships. Additionally, all component contributions to the CEV were examined in both the NMRK and MRK quark and antiquark splitting limits. In the latter case, the corresponding results match previous findings by Fadin and Kuraev for a six-gluon process. In the former case, and specifically within the more restricted BFKL quark and antiquark splitting limits, the two-gluon CEV can be described by a product of two BFKL vertices, allowing derivation of the impact factor for a six-gluon process directly from impact factors for single-emission processes. In the NMRK quark and antiquark splitting limits, the two-gluon CEV can be described as a product of two CEVs for single-emission processes, or equivalently as the sum of a CEV for single-emission processes and a BBKJT-type dispersive contribution. This latter finding has significant implications for the extension of the BBKJT equation to NNLL accuracy. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Lastly, we estimate that Rashba coupling's optimal magnitude required for these non-trivial topological properties may be achievable through material design. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The found evidence for this transition phenomenon may also be observable in other types of cuprate materials that are $d$-wave superconductors and could provide a key to understanding another phenomenon called pseudogap. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings are experimentally supported by images obtained through cryogenic scanning electron microscopy, revealing the intricate details of spherical brush microstructures. This research offers a fundamental theoretical framework for understanding surface-grafted polymer geometry and free energy calculations, potentially enabling the design of materials with tailored properties through the appropriate selection of surface curvatures and stretching strengths. By numerically solving these strong-stretching brush equations, we should be able to simulate a broad range of brush geometries, as demonstrated by our experimental validation using cryogenic scanning electron microscopy. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We examine how beta_k behavior changes when the shortest distance limit is increased and look at some specific graphs where their own individual behavior patterns are established, but for many graphs the paper is unable to determine their beta_k value despite it being known that all graphs have a defined beta_k. Additionally, the paper discusses a restricted version of this property where the points are limited to a specific sub-set and how it relates to the overall beta_k property. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Additionally, this method may facilitate easier comparison of images across different energy bands and help inform mission designers for next-generation gamma-ray telescopes. The team published their findings in an open-access paper available here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04810. The dictionary learning and U-net code have been made open-source and can be found at https://github.com/fermi-science/fskip_synthesis. The noise2noise code will be made available upon resolution of a copyright issue. The authors present their methodology and results in the accompanying paper. The all-sky maps used in this study are based on 8 years of data from the fermi latitude survey. The models' performance is evaluated through a set of tailored metrics, including structural similarity, frequency response, and spectral similarity. The team explored various configurations for the machine learning models, including different number of features in the dictionary and hidden units in the neural network, and showed that these details affect the results. The paper concludes by highlighting potential applications of this approach and future developments. The supplemental material contains additional figures and tables. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. This new metric assesses social welfare when employing action sequences over more efficient, dictatorially optimal approaches. We demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of our approach by applying it to various combinatorial optimization domains including graph matching and arborescence in directed graphs. When applying our approach to Boolean satisfiability, we developed a new algorithm for obtaining a $3$-approximation when considering Boolean satisfiability over general graphs. In contrast with traditional optimization methods based on sequence evaluation, our approach exhibits a significant expansion in computational complexity when dealing with domains that are inherently sequential in nature, such as arborescence in directed graphs. Nonetheless, our results indicate that obtaining a higher approximation ratio is achievable when employing our approach for Boolean satisfiability when comparing it with standard optimization methods based on sequence evaluation. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From the analysis of ~125,000 asteroids spanning nearly 70 million 
seconds of observation time, our top prospects included six marked asteroids, 
with profiles exhibiting enhanced mass ratios of up to 0.36±0.08, potentially 
identifying one to two wide binary asteroids for the first time. Due to the 
limited sample size, however, our findings require further confirmation, 
notably through high-resolution imaging, to solidify our discoveries. If 
validated, our detections would not only increase the known roster of binary 
asteroids but also empower researchers to reconstruct the binary asteroids' 
orbital paths. Lastly, as wide binary asteroids hold significant importance, we 
encourage astronomers to prioritize them in future surveys and observational 
programs. If our results are indicative of a larger population of wide binary 
asteroids, future research could be guided by the established statistics, 
else further study will be needed to fully understand these binary asteroids. 
In either case, continuing to prioritize and study wide binary asteroids is 
crucial. Additionally, I intend to share open-access archival data, along with 
analysis code, for further examination and potential binary asteroid detections.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  It also explains why the Brazilian margin has more varied crust than the West African, since the latter has sections of ancient Rio Grande Craton.  It further indicates that conjugate passive margins are not always exact mirror images.  It also enables the prediction of structurally complex areas like the S~ao Paulo High, to be accurate to within 50 km, and shows that break-up histories that are multi-velocity and multi-directional, have a significant impact on conjugate passive margins.  It also means that break-up histories as complex as this one, may be more common than previously thought, occurring in other rift systems such as East Africa and the Arabian-Nubian board.  It also provides a challenge to models of break-up at conjugate margins, that assume similar velocities and directions, and suggests that break-up models for conjugate margins, need to be unique to each individual case, as such a complex history, could result in break-up patterns, that may vary significantly, even when two continents are breaking apart in opposite directions, since the analysis has shown, that velocity and direction, can change over time, with implications for processes, that occur during break-up, such as magmatism, faulting and craton break

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. To facilitate comparison and replication, our study makes use of publicly available datasets and pre-trained models. Furthermore, both type-based and token-based approaches are easily adaptable to other languages with minimal modifications, thanks to their reliance on general corpus characteristics. Overall, our study provides substantial evidence for the feasibility and accuracy of both type-based and token-based approaches in facilitating discovery of new words with evolving meanings within a corpus. Moreover, our study paves the way for further exploration of lexical semantic change discovery in near-future large language datasets. Nonetheless, there are still concerns that our type-based approach may be susceptible to inaccuracies, as evidenced by lower F1 scores in specific cases. Consequently, there is a growing need for additional research aimed at fully validating the accuracy of both type-based and token-based methods on a broader range of datasets and potential use cases. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. With further study, it's hoped that the unique properties of Heusler compounds synthesized through remote epitaxy can be explored. Due to the intricate relationships between process conditions, materials properties and atomic arrangements, a comprehensive theoretical simulation was necessary to provide a clear understanding of this unique rotation phenomenon. This knowledge may also contribute to developing strategies for achieving remote epitaxy on single-layer graphene on an insulating substrate. It's concluded that when considering remote epitaxy on graphene, it's not sufficient to simply claim a remote epitaxial relationship; rather a comprehensive analysis involving transmission electron microscopy, energy dispersion spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy and theoretical simulations is required to fully understand the atomic arrangements and process conditions necessary for this process. Furthermore, this study highlights the challenges associated with achieving remote epitaxy on graphene and the necessity for a precise definition of this term. Due to these complexities, it's not surprising that there is a significant discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental findings in the field of Heusler compounds. To move forward, it's essential to unify the terminology by precisely defining remote epitaxy, followed by a robust investigation of this process in multiple research groups. In the context of this study, remote epitaxy refers to a process where a film lattice structures are identical to those of the substrate, alongside a rotation of the film's atomic arrangement on the substrate. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. We show that the categorification of the Haag-Kastler axioms, incorporating this relationship, results in a set of axioms that are equivalent to a specific formulation of the Chu d'Alembert theorem. Furthermore, we prove that the algebraic QFT scheme, characterized by the Haag-Kastler axioms, derives its underlying structure solely from this relationship, independent of specific algebraic details. This implies that the behavior of physical systems remains consistent across different algebraic structures, as the relationship serves as the underlying bridge between physical properties and the structure of these algebras. We also explore the role of anti-algebras and Jones algebras in this framework, demonstrating that they represent fundamental aspects of the underlying physics. This understanding, in turn, provides the basis for recognizing the role of topological invariants in algebraic QFT. We conclude that the abstract relationship between physical states and observables serves as the primary source of the algebraic structure's underlying properties, meaning that this structure can be seen as an explicit manifestation of the fundamental principles of the Haag-Kastler axioms. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Additionally, we establish a lower bound and an upper bound for the sequence
reconstruction problem when r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate that both these bounds become equal when r = 4 and a
distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r, or in cases where d exceeds r.
As a result, we derive a specific formula for the sequence reconstruction problem
when r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
On the other hand, we determine that no two spheres with centers that are at least d
units apart will ever intersect in a metric with a radius r, or in cases where d
exceeds r. 
Consequently, the optimal solution for the sequence reconstruction problem occurs
when one of the spheres is entirely contained within the other. 
Therefore, the problem of finding the least amount of transmission channels needed
to obtain an accurate replica of the original transmitted sequence reduces to
determining the number of unique entries within the contained sphere.
With this understanding, we derive specific formulas for all possible combinations
of r and d that fit the criteria of being at least 2 and not exceeding 4. 
These formulas provide a clear framework for identifying the required number
