The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technologies. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator. To date, both GECAM satellites have detected natural GRBs from space. Moreover, the GRB simulator has facilitated the demonstration of several key features, including the dependence of photon flux on gravitational wave detection software, the distribution of photon energies, and the detection capabilities of the GRDs' front-end and onboard computer. Furthermore, this simulator has enabled the simulation of GRBs during space environment simulation tests to validate the performance of the GRDs in orbit. Additionally, the GRB simulator has also facilitated the demonstration of several GRB detection scenarios, such as front-end-only detection, onboard software-only detection, and combined detection, as well as the determination of the satellites' relative orientation. Moreover, this simulator has allowed the execution of sophisticated software tests, including the calculation of coordinates, time tagging, and the conversion of data formats. Moreover, the GRB simulator has also facilitated the transmission of detected GRBs to ground stations, the generation of alert messages, and the delivery of raw and packed data to scientists in real-time. Overall, the performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator has been validated before launch, and both GECAM satellites have successfully detected natural GRBs from space. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
The updated version maintains consistency with the original designs, incorporating all initial settings, objects, and actions commonly found in text-based games. 
To facilitate seamless integration with existing research tools, we've created a backward-compatible API that works across multiple programming languages, including Python, C++, and Java. 
The optimized code is publicly available for download, providing researchers and developers a free resource to conduct thorough, time-efficient tests of their agents. 
With improved performance now within reach, we expect a significant expansion in the scope and precision of future evaluations conducted on text-based game challenges. 
The time has come for the community to reconsider previously held assumptions about the limitations of system performance and memory usage in text-based games, as our research has demonstrated the potential for substantial upgrades, at minimal development costs. 
As a result, we strongly advise all practitioners to review their methods for detecting algorithmic improvements, as our findings may already be affected by an incomplete understanding of the current performance landscape. 
On the technical side, our optimization achievements were made possible by a combination of several advanced development strategies, including the creation of a custom fast VM, a lock-free in-memory database, and a multithreaded interactive command-line interface, each of which has the potential to contribute positively to the performance of other text-based games. 
Finally, we've taken the opportunity to redesign the instruction manual for setting up the test environment, simplifying it to make it even easier for others to replicate our research methodology. 
As the field of text-based games continues to evolve, we are confident that the efficiency gains achieved with TextWorldExpress will give a necessary boost to the further development of robust evaluation methods. 
On the practical side, our research has already led to the detection of a major flaw in one popular algorithm that was previously believed to have achieved optimal results but was actually performance-optimized for an earlier version of the game, and we anticipate this finding

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The study also examined the behavior of agent-specific learning algorithms, discovering that, when learning is effective, agents exploit market power, but, when learning is less efficient, agents are prone to sandboarding due to explicit design. The model and study results can contribute to the development of evidence-based policy designs for the electricity sector. Additionally, the model can be expanded to address other design issues in the electricity sector. Finally, the model is built with modular, open-source components that are easily integratable with other agent-based models, such as the PyPSA-PFA model. The model is made available on the GitHub platform for users and developers. Developers can develop new design options and policy performance indicators, and contribute to the model improvement. The name of this model is Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM). ASAM model is highly compatible with the PyPSA-PFA model, and they share the same market design parameters, agent-specific learning algorithms, and policy performance indicators. Both models are part of the suite of high-performance agent-based models for designing and analyzing multi-agent systems, such as power systems, networks of road users, and financial networks, among others. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Theoretical proofs are supported by examples using the Frobenius automorphism and the twisted Fermat curve. The analysis of the Galois group's behavior with increasing degree appears to conform to the universal principle that complex dynamics follow. The framework established in this paper can be further expanded to composite polynomials of multiple variables, potentially opening the door for exploration in this area. Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions may be more complex, involving significant excitations on a long-time scale. We also provide an exact finite-size scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states, which can be used to investigate the crossover from quasi-condensation to BEC on the edge of an attractive 1D Bose gas. This edge case is particularly significant because it allows a direct comparison with our findings for quantum double dark-soliton states. Additionally, we analyze the dynamics of these states during a uniform phase shift, and demonstrate a universal quasi-condensation peak in time-dependent density profiles for an interacting boson gas. This peak represents a fundamental dynamics component that arises from the response of quasi-condensation to the shift, and its intensity is directly proportional to the fraction of BEC in the ground state. We also show that notches in these profiles will always deepen over time due to a phase lead in excitations relative to the condensate. This phenomenon results in a long-time crossover from a quasi-condensation dominated regime to one dominated by the edge of a attractive 1D Bose gas, where a similar notch deepens in response to a smaller shift. This behavior leads to a critical time for a system that can be scaled by BEC fraction. We further demonstrate that this crossover can be controlled by adjusting the number of atoms in the system. Furthermore, we investigate the dynamics of these states during a local phase shift, and observe a universal quasi-condensation peak in time-dependent density profiles for an interacting boson gas.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Furthermore, this method may be adaptable to other interferometric experiments that involve scattering processes. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. Additionally, this framework may facilitate the exploration of novel quantum error threshold values, as well as a deeper understanding of how fault-tolerant quantum computing performance scales with system size, particularly in scenarios involving large numbers of faulty gates and the subsequent accumulation of error over time. We further apply this framework to investigate the performance of quantum circuit learning algorithms, demonstrating how fault-tolerant quantum computing could be achieved through the incorporation of quantum learning elements that facilitate reliable outcome interpretations, even in the presence of experience-based training noise. Finally, we utilize this framework to examine the error tolerance of a recently proposed quantum algorithm for simulating the dynamics of overhauser disordered systems, and we find that its performance falls short of the optimal result achieved by a conventional classical simulation, primarily due to the limited size of the quantum register and the occurrence of stable state faults during circuit execution. However, we believe that fault-tolerant versions of this algorithm may still hold promise for addressing certain computational challenges. We have made this research openly available in the hope that it may contribute to the advancement of fault-tolerant quantum learning and learning from quantum data, and we invite feedback and suggestions on future research collaborations. We intend to explore potential collaborations with institutions and organizations involved in the development of near-term quantum technology, with a focus on fault-tolerant quantum learning and learning from quantum data, and we welcome the opportunity to work with collaborative groups on these topics. We anticipate that successful outcomes from these research efforts could lead to further funding and resource allocation for our research team, and we are confident that they will make a significant contribution to the field of fault-tolerant quantum learning and learning from quantum data

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  This energy barrier originates from a local distortion in the diamond lattice caused by the presence of the nitrogen-vacancy center.  We also observed a significant decrease in the proportion of emitted photons that are not resonant with the diamond, and attributed this to a combination of temperature-dependent effects on the diamond and nearby nitrogen vacancies.  Furthermore, under high-temperature and vacuum conditions, we detected a prominent resonance frequency at approximately 1.42 gigahertz in ODMR spectra, whose intensity decreases with rising temperature.  By analyzing these results, we propose that the resonance frequency at high temperatures may be explained by a combination of temperature-dependent effects on the diamond and nearby nitrogen vacancies, although the implications of these findings require further investigation.  Additionally, by exploring the effects of different nitrogen vacancies on the diamond's optical properties, we gathered evidence that the nonradiative energy barrier in these centers varies depending on their composition, a finding that could have implications for the development of nitrogen-vacancy based technology.  Finally, by comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we found that this theory accurately captures the temperature-dependent effects on the frequencies of ODMR resonance, but falls short of explaining the observed shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  To further elucidate this phenomenon, we developed a quantum simulation of the diamond's electronic structure, and discovered that it exhibits a nonlinear response to increasing temperature. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. Notably, this method was found to be superior to traditional methods in terms of stability and convergence, requiring significantly fewer basis functions to achieve comparable accuracy. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our approach and data are publicly available for further research. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this shortfall, the model is modified to incorporate a non-local epidemiological approach, which incorporates the city's subway system to facilitate more agile population movement. This revised model is then used to make predictions regarding the temporal aspects of the disturbances, which are validated through satisfactory statistical comparisons with historical data. Furthermore, the model is adapted to analyze the underlying causes of the disorders using an epidemiological approach, which enables the identification of key variables influencing disorderly behavior and their associated policy implications. This modified model is applicable to other complex systems characterized by interconnected sub-regions and non-immediate population movement patterns. It is hypothesized that this revised model can further improve its accuracy regarding the spatial distribution of riots by incorporating additional data on Santiago's population, as well as potential modifications to the model's underlying epidemiological principles. This project is a theoretical exploration aimed at developing a practical application, as the current formulation is not designed to make specific policy recommendations for Chilean policymakers. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Furthermore, our model proves to be not only more accurate but also more prone to external influences such as light fluctuations and minor sensor errors, resulting in a more robust pose estimation. The proposed model achieves an average error of 4.57 cm without the influence of light, and 6.29 cm with light affecting the estimates, while the current state-of-the-art VIO baseline achieved an average error of 5.12 cm and 7.15 cm in these conditions, respectively. The model's performance in various scenarios, along with its training and evaluation processes, is illustrated through a mobile robotics application video, available online. The framework's code is also openly available for public use. The challenges faced by learning-based VIO models in regards to their limited training data, compared to the vast amount of image data available, further highlight the need to develop more efficient and robust models capable of handling a wider range of scenes and environments. The proposed EMA-VIO framework addresses these concerns by enhancing the efficiency and performance of both the pose estimation and learning algorithms, resulting in more accurate and robust results. The model's external memory and attention learning components enable it to process and utilize the data from both the camera and inertial sensors more effectively, while minimizing the necessity for recurrent models in the learning algorithm. The code for the proposed EMA-VIO framework is available online, along with the evaluation video illustrating its performance. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, FedSA excels in simplifying complex models by incorporating looser constraints, reducing the risk of adverse outcomes like neural network neutrality. The code for our experiments is publicly available on the FedSA GitHub repository. Additionally, we introduce the Image- FedSA Benchmark, a pioneering platform that enables the evaluation of FedSA models across various tasks and networks. This benchmark includes a diverse collection of teacher models, along with corresponding data sources and training protocols, to support the assessment of FedSA models in real-world scenarios. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, we will discuss prominent theoretical models proposed to explain grid cells' characteristics and the circuits that govern their behavior. With its comprehensive review of the current state of grid cell research, this survey aims to provide a valuable resource for both established experts in the field and newcomers seeking to understand the intricate world of grid cells. In addition, we hope to facilitate further discussion and debate on various unresolved aspects related to grid cells through the inclusion of open problems and key questions. As the field of grid cell research continues to evolve, we anticipate that this survey will serve as a useful platform for presenting novel findings and novel perspectives on grid cells in the future. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. As a result, we suggest that observational indicators of magnetic cycles, such as X-ray emission and chromospheric activity, are insufficient for confirming cycles in these stars. Instead, we propose utilizing the relationship between rotational modulation and orbital period, as described by the equatorial rotational modulation period, and evaluating the magnetic cycle period through a hybrid approach combining traditional BL-TT and kinematic dynamo simulations. If stars spend enough time in the slow rotor phase, their magnetic cycle periods may be substantially longer than their rotational periods, making cycles more difficult to detect. Additionally, we suggest that dynamic simulations exploring a wider range of initial conditions and parameters be conducted, in order to fully understand the behavior of these dynamos throughout a solar-type star's lifetime. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. The performance of upper bounds was evaluated for random sets of nodes. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of utilizing mid-infrared pump-probe techniques to directly monitor the effects of microwave exposure on the local carrier concentration and dielectric properties. This integrated approach involving near-field terahertz studies and pump-probe experiments has the potential to provide valuable insights into the interaction between microwave fields and the surrounding material, ultimately facilitating the optimization of quantum devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pump-probe experiments can be used to assess the impact of microwave exposure on specific locations, while near-field terahertz studies offer a means to investigate the global properties of these regions, making them equally important for the development of quantum technology. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. Furthermore, this method displays potential in accurately identifying tumor invasive front regions, which is an area of ongoing research. In conclusion, this study contributes a ground-breaking approach to modeling tissues and highlights the advantages of utilizing a hierarchical graph representation, which has implications beyond cancer research that relies on histology. The source code for this study is made available on GitHub at https://github.com/jjz1117/HACT-Net. Additionally, the BRACS dataset can be accessed through UM-breast cancer dataset on GitHub at https://github.com/jjz1117/UM-breast-cancer-dataset. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This research builds upon previous work, such as the studies on Bayesian estimation of linear models and the sparse nonlinear Hawkes process, making the Bayesian approach a more well-rounded solution for analyzing and understanding complex point processes that capture interconnections and interactions between events of different types. 
  We have also explored a novel technique for handling a significant challenge in estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process: the thin data stream issue. The proposed solution involves combining data from multiple sources that share a similar underlying structure, utilities a new concentration inequality, and demonstrates the benefits of this approach through simulations and real-world applications. 
  The data stream problem remains an area for further research, as does the investigation of new Bayesian methodologies such as sampling algorithms and predictive checks. The extensive theoretical foundations established in this research provide a sturdy ground for exploring more intricate Bayesian models that can capture the complex dynamics and interactions between events of different types.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through pairwise and single-step test cases, including scenarios modeling collapsing neutron stars and binary neutron star mergers. Our results compare favourably to direct $N$-body integration, showcasing that FMM-based simulations preserve key dynamical properties for multiple steps. As such, our modified FMM can serve as a feasible and accurate hybrid $N$-body solver for a broad spectrum of computational astrophysical applications. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. The project's code is available online at https://github.com/putuebin/CS-CADA. The findings are also visually illustrated in an accompanying video available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QD3jK9j6bQY. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Notwithstanding this, our research paves the way for exploring low-rank factorization methods in single-source piano transcriptions. The source code is publicly available online. Moreover, we introduce an open-source tool for evaluating piano translations, referred to as PianoAlign. This evaluation utility is designed for both command-line and graphical interface use. Furthermore, we make the preprocessed MAPS dataset, including individual note recordings, freely accessible for download. These preprocessed data serve as a foundation for further piano transcription research. Additionally, we outline several promising research directions for exploring our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method and low-rank factorization techniques in general. Finally, we highlight the necessity for larger-scale annotated datasets consisting of multiple audio recordings of each individual note to facilitate more comprehensive evaluations. These recordings could be obtained through a straightforward listening task. This heightened interpretability enables a more in-depth analysis of the factorized matrix components, encompassing both the basis elements and the coefficient matrix. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. Our numerical simulations for barotropic evolution show comparable results to existing general-relativity studies, while novel applications, including the evolution of protostars and neon-white-dwarf internal dynamics, are also explored. Furthermore, we have extracted oscillation modes from our formulations, aligning with previous general-relativity studies, and have discovered early signs of baroclinic instability developing in rotating stars. 

Our new framework is highly adaptable, allowing for the incorporation of a user-defined equation of state functions, potential applications such as the study of pulsational and explosive phenomena, and potential extensions, including the exploration of stellar mergers and protostar collapse. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, we found that models trained with selective labeling performed on par with those trained using fully labeled datasets, according to various evaluation metrics. Our code is now available on GitHub under the MIT License. Our research lays the groundwork for exploring cost-effective document annotation methods that can accommodate large datasets. Additionally, we believe that selective labeling has broader implications for addressing high labeling costs in visual object detection applications. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the scope for further improvement, where future training on larger datasets incorporating multiple detectors and diverse signal orientations presents significant potential for enhanced performance. In turn, this could enable the detection of multiple merging binary neutron star events, such as the one identified through electromagnetic radiation following the event GW170817. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the efficacy of deep learning techniques in comparing traditional methods, providing a foundational framework for further innovation and future advances in multi-messenger astronomy. With the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors like the next-generation laser interferometer detectors, our approach will be crucial in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required to fully utilize their full detection capacity. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Ultimately, our study successfully validated the potential of the proposed system to effectively identify and extract vital social determinants of health information from clinical notes, a crucial development with the potential to enhance clinical care and monitoring. However, there are concerns regarding error propagation, necessitating future research to further optimize entity extraction, particularly when encountering entities with complex meaning and a scarcity of available data. Additionally, there is a need to incorporate context from surrounding sections or notes, as well as addressing issues related to privacy and data governance. As the field progresses, there is a opportunity to utilize extensively annotated data to train models for a variety of critical tasks, such as predicting clinical outcomes, building referral systems, and tracking patient progress. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This could pave the way for redefining the kilogram in terms of atomic constants through the measurement of these field strengths. A demonstration of this principle can be seen in the accompanying figure, which graphically represents atomic interference patterns before and after placing a superconductor near one of the atomic paths. As expected, magnetic field expulsion resulted in increased frequency modulation, confirmed by a accuracy of $10^{-3}$ in a initial test. Further optimization is needed to fulfill the required sensitivity. As this detection method offers a non-invasive approach without the need to access the superconductor, it has implications for the validation of quantum states within complex superconducting devices. Furthermore, this method can be expanded to accurately measure magnetic fields generated by non-localized currents by utilizing a thin superconducting wire and modifying the atomic interferometry setup accordingly. This development holds significant potential for the advancement of atomic physics and magnetic field measurement technology. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. However, this equivalence holds only in the case of very narrow gaps. We also analyze the implications of these findings on design choices for gap-plasmon resonances. Moreover, we observe that the hydrodynamics model exhibits better convergence than the Thomas-Fermi model, which could be attributed to its longer mean free path or more precise representation of the electric field's response. Nonetheless, both descriptions still fall short of accurately capturing the actual behavior within just a few nanometers. Nonetheless, for even smaller gap sizes, both models overestimate the impact of spillover, suggesting that another effect becomes dominant at this scale. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Additionally, DynaSOAr's memory management efficiency is proven in tests, where it shows a notable reduction in memory management overhead, demonstrating its superiority over standard memory allocators.  As an open-source framework, DynaSOAr is readily available for download at its official GitHub repository https://github.com/CSalehD/DynaSOAr, where developers can find detailed information on its implementation, as well as guidance on using its memory allocator and data layout DSL.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr is included in the CUDA toolkit as a demonstration application for CUDA Development Tool kit.  Finally, several real-world applications are successfully parallelized using DynaSOAr, further proving the feasibility of object-oriented programming on SIMD devices.  As a result, software developers are now free to easily parallelize any object-oriented application on SIMD devices using DynaSOAr.  As such, DynaSOAr is considered a milestone in bridging the historical gap between object-oriented programming and high-performance computing on SIMD devices. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. These findings contribute significantly to the understanding of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material and the YSR states they give rise to. Moreover, this research demonstrates the potential of this theoretical framework to investigate a wide range of magnetic systems located on the surface of a superconducting material. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Furthermore, FourierMask shows substantial improvement over Mask R-CNN at higher resolutions on the PASCAL 3D R dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/AmirGayfer/FourierMask.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron void. Additionally, our experiment features an auxiliary thin layer with low density, situated behind the main target layer. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated into a mono-energetic beam by the electrostatic field generated in the main target under interaction with a negatively frequency-modulated, highly intense laser pulse, achieving protons with maximum energies of around 100 MeV when subjected to specific optimal conditions involving a 10-fs, intensively Gaussian pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak intensity. Conversely, positively frequency-modulated pulses hinder ion acceleration due to field reversal before the electron void forms. The absence of behind-the-target ion acceleration in cases of positive frequency variations is also validated by 2D particle-in-cell simulations utilizing an accurately modeled, negatively frequency-modulated 10-fs pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak power. Nonetheless, accelerated ions still exhibit significant energies, mainly resulting from field formation at the target front due to the intense electric field at the leading edge of the positively frequency-modulated pulse. Furthermore, our research indicates that the occurrence of relativistic self-induced transparency in the target can lead to increased transmission at higher density regimes, potentially expanding the applications of this phenomenon to study high-density plasma interaction with intense, short laser pulses. Additionally, our findings may also imply that negative frequency variations facilitate a broader range of stable, persistent electrostatic fields generated in interaction with intense, short laser pulses, offering a greater potential for ion acceleration across a wider range of target densities. Consequently, this research may provide a groundwork for exploring new strategies to achieve efficient multi-MeV ion acceleration in future experiments

The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS, and our analysis suggests that N dimerizes with oxygen rather than Ti.  Moreover, we find that both carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We believe that optimizing detection methods for these defects could significantly enhance the performance of TiO2 based photo-detecting devices. Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy. X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzing these quantities, measurements are constrained by instrumental uncertainties and the inherent variability in cosmic observations. Here, the formalism established in a previous paper is expanded to account for the statistical uncertainty in line diagnostics, specifically structure functions. Statistical variance contributes to total variance in several ways, influenced by the detector's geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of turbulent fields. These terms hold significant importance for studying turbulence at smaller scales. A demonstration is conducted for the X-IFU using a simulated turbulent velocity map of a galaxy cluster resembling Coma. Results indicate excellent agreement with theoretical formulas for structure function estimation and its associated variance. These derived expressions can be applied to any X-ray measurement of turbulent structure functions and provide a framework for optimizing future instrumentation and observational strategies. Furthermore, these formulas can be used to create mock data for model evaluation and likelihood calculations during model parameter estimation. In the context of the X-IFU, its response to turbulent velocity maps will be a key factor in the recovery of true structure function values. In the Coma-like cluster scenario, with an observed scale of a few hundred kiloparsecs, the instrumental variance dominates the total variance. However, below this scale, the statistical variance dominates the total variance. Optimizing instrumental variance involves a balance between increasing the count rate, achieved through a higher exposure time but at the cost of motion blur, or improving the spatial resolution, with a better-defined resolution requiring a shorter exposure time but resulting in a decreased count rate. An instrumental variance reduction by a factor of five can recover detail by one factor in length, but this depends on the specific conditions and variance components. For the X-IFU, a trade-off between the pixelation and the fraction of out-of-bandlight scattering does not significantly impact variance for typical observations. However, further optimization of the instrument's response to turbulent velocity maps, particularly considering the effect of binning, is necessary to fully explore its potential in studying ICM turbulence. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Moreover, this research explores the relationship between the diameter and some dynamic groups' properties, such as their growth rate and diameter in variational form. This includes a result similar to Gilman's recent finding on the groups with the smallest possible diameter that scale cubically. This research also includes some examples and nonconstructive proofs of the existence of groups meeting certain criteria. Finally, some open questions related to the diameter of finite groups are discussed. This research builds on previous work by Breuillard, Tointon, and Gilman.

Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. Additionally, we discovered that slight fluctuations in stable stratification can prolong the onset of instability in the axisymmetric mode. This finding implies that stars requiring a long period of stability, such as white dwarfs, likely maintain stable stratification throughout their interior. In contrast, stars that experience a different internal process, like tidal generation, may still support stable configurations, as the condition for these configurations does not impose restrictions on the magnetic energy produced. These results contribute valuable insights to the ongoing debate about the stability of global magnetic fields within stars. Furthermore, they establish a framework for resolving this issue through numerical simulations, given a deeper understanding of the internal processes occurring within these stars. In addition, we explore potential observations that can test these theoretical predictions, specifically, the relationship between magnetic fields and the stellar rotation rate, potential fluctuations in the stable stratification, and the generation of the magnetic field. Lastly, we explore potential connections between these processes and phenomena such as magnetic braking, stellar oscillations, and the generation of the magnetic field. This knowledge could offer valuable insights into the process of massive star formation, along with the associated formation of massive prestellar cores. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. It also discusses the Chalmers-Lewis-style approach to definable sets of formulas, resulting in an order isomorphism between the set of formulas and the set of definable sets for some of these Godel modal logics. The research is shown to include well-known intutionistic modal logics such as S1S and BIS within its family of Godel modal logics. The study focuses on the interplay between single and double accessibility relations in its relational frames, ensuring that no new outcomes arise from a given set of formulas when switching from a single to a double relation. The study is explored further through an online database containing numerous technical results, including algebraic and relational semantics for various subvarieties of finite Godel modal algebras. The research is primarily math-based, addressing topics in the field of mathematical logic. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Furthermore, we find that using a dimension reduction technique like a fully connected encoder yields superior classification accuracy across all methods we tested. Our research establishes a foundation for further exploration into the classification of LiDAR data, primarily focusing on the use of context-based information and advanced dimension reduction techniques. We conclude by highlighting potential research extensions, specifically considering the application of implicit encoders and auxiliary classification for improved performance. Our research findings are supported by 12 figures and 4 additional tables. We hope our work to be a valuable reference for any scholar considering the classification of LiDAR data. With that in mind, we wish to express our willingness to engage in any further discussion that may arise from any claim made in our research. Our research was conducted with the support of the University of Oulu's Visual Inference Group and the Oulu University Centre for Electronics, Electrical Engineering. Additionally, we wish to extend our gratitude to Dr. Jian Li for his valuable insights and guidance throughout this research. Our team consists of three members: Olli Raita acted as the primary supervisor, Dr. Jian Li served as the secondary supervisor, and Jouni Himanen contributed his expertise as both a supervisor and a co-author. Our research team collectively holds expertise in the fields of computer science, statistics, and forestry, enabling us to approach the classification of LiDAR data from diverse perspectives. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations. Additionally, we present results on neutrino-UHECR pairs, which provide superior sensitivity to spatial correlations, significantly reducing the predicted abundance of such pairs compared to previous estimates. The analyses' methods are equally applicable to future neutrino and UHECR detectors. With anticipated upgrades, discovering neutrino-UHECR correlations should become feasible as early as 2025. The upgraded analysis for neutrino-UHECR pairs can already reach the predicted rates from known sources with a significance of approximately 3σ by 2025. Furthermore, it is expected that in the future with significantly enhanced data sets, searching for UHECR-neutrino pairs on larger scales will become a primary method to identify sources of UHECRs and neutrinos. The future effectiveness of this approach relies on accurately identifying source locations in proportion to the predicted spatial distributions. The outcomes presented in this research extend beyond neutrino-UHECR connections, offering a framework to pinpoint multi-direction UHECR sources and better comprehend the physics underlying cosmic ray physics.
